title: Units: whole minor units per currency code, the currency table and its fallback, 26 or 27 pays a year spread so the year adds up, interest rounded half up, monthly amounts per pay
written_in: SCHEMA_V3 0, 3 (interest), 8 (units), 11 (the move's questions); DECISIONS_ROUND2 B4, B8, H9, I2, J1, E2
notes: Every amount is made up. Inputs typed by a person are text ("19.99"); everything else is whole minor units: yen 1 is 1, peso 1.00 is 100.

Question `to_minor`: a typed amount in a currency, as whole minor units with the currency's decimals and whether the screen must ask about the code. Question `currency_for`: the code from what an old copy or a person gave, or ask. Question `interest`: one month's interest on a balance at a yearly rate in percent [I2]. Question `pays_in_year`: the real number of pays a schedule has in a calendar year [H9]. Question `per_pay`: a monthly amount over that many pays, shown as the low and high per-pay amounts, how many get the high one, and the year's total. Question `period_amount`: what one pay period gets for a budget line or Free to spend by its `per` [B8]. Question `by_day`: with no fixed pay, what a monthly amount comes to over a number of days [B4].

cases.question: to_minor
cases.title: Yen has no decimals: 1 yen is 1
cases.why: Section 0: yen 1 is 1. The table gives JPY 0 decimals.

cases.question: to_minor
cases.title: Pesos have two decimals: 1.00 is 100
cases.why: Section 0: peso 1.00 is 100. PHP has 2 decimals, so 1 x 100 + 00 = 100.

cases.question: to_minor
cases.title: 19.99 pesos is 1999, read from the text
cases.why: 19 x 100 + 99 = 1,999. Worked as a decimal number, 19.99 x 100 is 1998.9999999999998, so a reader that cuts off instead of rounding would store 1,998. The digits are read as text.

cases.question: to_minor
cases.title: 0.29 pesos is 29

cases.question: to_minor
cases.title: One decimal typed in a two-decimal currency
cases.why: USD has 2 decimals (the table in lookahead_ref.js): 1,234 x 100 + 50 = 123,450. ".5" is fifty cents.

cases.question: to_minor
cases.title: An unknown code: 2 decimals, and the screen asks once
cases.why: Section 0: an unknown code is 2 decimals and the screen asks once. 12 x 100 + 34 = 1,234, with ask set.

cases.question: currency_for
cases.title: A code is used as it is
cases.why: Every account, schedule, goal and budget line carries an ISO code (section 0); a code needs no question.

cases.question: currency_for
cases.title: "$" is asked, never guessed
cases.why: Section 0 and 11: "$" (dollars of many countries, and pesos are written with it too) is asked, never guessed.

cases.question: currency_for
cases.title: "¥" is asked, never guessed
cases.why: "¥" is yen or yuan; section 0 says it is asked.

cases.question: currency_for
cases.title: An old copy with no currency is asked, never set to pesos
cases.why: H9: old copies with no currency are asked, never set to pesos (the old default). The question comes before any amount is turned into minor units (section 11), because the decimals depend on it.

cases.question: interest
cases.title: 100,000 yen at 15% a year: 1,250 for the month

cases.question: interest
cases.title: 93,000 yen at 15%: half a yen rounds up
cases.why: 93,000 x 15 / 1,200 = 1,162.5. Half up to the minor unit gives 1,163 [I2]. (The same figure as interest.json's carried 93,000.)

cases.question: interest
cases.title: 123.45 pesos at 18%: under half a centavo rounds down
cases.why: 12,345 centavos x 18 / 1,200 = 185.175 centavos. The part after the minor unit is .175, under half, so 185 (1.85 pesos).

cases.question: interest
cases.title: A rate with a decimal: 14.6%

cases.question: interest
cases.title: Exactly half a minor unit goes up
cases.why: 100 x 6 / 1,200 = 0.5. Half up gives 1. Worked in whole numbers, so no decimal number can land just under 0.5.

cases.question: interest
cases.title: Under half a minor unit is nothing
cases.why: 1 x 6 / 1,200 = 0.005, under half of one minor unit, so 0.

cases.question: interest
cases.title: A credit carries no interest
cases.why: A balance at or below zero is a credit; J confirms no interest on a credit.

cases.question: pays_in_year
cases.title: Every two weeks from Fri 1 Jan 2027: 27 pays in 2027
cases.why: 1 Jan + 14 x 26 days = 1 Jan + 364 days = Fri 31 Dec 2027, still in 2027. So 1 + 26 = 27 pays [H9].

cases.question: pays_in_year
cases.title: Every two weeks from Fri 8 Jan 2027: 26 pays
cases.why: 8 Jan + 14 x 25 = 8 Jan + 350 days = Fri 24 Dec 2027; the next, 7 Jan 2028, is in the next year. 1 + 25 = 26.

cases.question: pays_in_year
cases.title: A schedule that started in 2026 keeps its rhythm in 2027
cases.why: From Fri 13 Nov 2026: 27 Nov, 11 Dec, 25 Dec 2026, then Fri 8 Jan 2027 is the first in 2027. As units-19: 26 pays in 2027.

cases.question: pays_in_year
cases.title: Weekly on Fridays: 53 pays in 2027
cases.why: 2027 starts on a Friday and has 365 days = 52 weeks + 1 day, so it has 53 Fridays: 1 Jan to 31 Dec. Section 8 says the real number of pays in that year; lookahead_ref.js uses 52 as its plain form, which is why this rule has its own file.

cases.question: pays_in_year
cases.title: Twice a month: 24 pays
cases.why: Two days in every month (31 is the last day in shorter months, 10.8): 12 x 2 = 24.

cases.question: per_pay
cases.title: 30,000 yen a month over 26 pays: the year adds up to 360,000
cases.why: 30,000 x 12 / 26 = 13,846.15. Every pay gets 13,846 or 13,847. 13,846 x 26 = 359,996, so 360,000 - 359,996 = 4 pays get the one extra yen and the year adds up exactly to 360,000 [H9]. (Which 4 is open question units-q4.)

cases.question: per_pay
cases.title: The same 30,000 a month in a 27-pay year
cases.why: 360,000 / 27 = 13,333.33. 13,333 x 27 = 359,991; 360,000 - 359,991 = 9 pays get 13,334. Each pay is smaller than in a 26-pay year, but the year is the same 360,000. Using 26 in a 27-pay year would plan 13,846 x 27 = 373,842, about 4% too much.

cases.question: per_pay
cases.title: 300.01 pesos a month, paid twice a month
cases.why: 30,001 centavos x 12 = 360,012 over 24 pays = 15,000.5. 15,000 x 24 = 360,000, so 12 pays get 15,001 and the year is 360,012 centavos (3,600.12 pesos), 12 times the month.

cases.question: per_pay
cases.title: When it divides exactly, every pay is the same

cases.question: period_amount
cases.title: `per: pay` gets its amount each pay
cases.why: Section 8: a period gets the amount when `per` matches its kind. Every period is a pay period, so a per-pay line gets 20,000.

cases.question: period_amount
cases.title: `per: month` with monthly pay gets its amount, however long the period
cases.why: Monthly pay, monthly line: `per` matches, so 60,000 whether the period is 28 or 33 days (schema_review_1: never spread by days for a monthly earner).

cases.question: period_amount
cases.title: `per: week` over a 31-day period
cases.why: Section 8: `week` gets amount x days / 7 = 7,000 x 31 / 7 = 31,000.

cases.question: period_amount
cases.title: `per: week` with weekly pay
cases.why: A 7-day period: 5,000 x 7 / 7 = 5,000, the same as `per` matching.

cases.question: by_day
cases.title: No fixed pay: a monthly amount comes off by day
cases.why: Section 8 and B4: the monthly amount x 12 / 365 a day = 36,500 x 12 / 365 = 1,200 a day; 30 days = 36,000.

open.question: What is in the currency table beyond JPY (0) and PHP (2), and from what source? ISO 4217 also has KRW and VND with 0 decimals and KWD and BHD with 3.
open.ref_does: a short ISO 4217 list: JPY, KRW, VND 0; PHP, USD, EUR, GBP, CHF, CAD, AUD, SGD 2; KWD, BHD 3

open.question: A typed amount with more decimals than its currency ("1234.5" yen, "12.345" pesos): refused, or rounded? Section 0 only says nothing is rounded on load.

"Pays in that year": the calendar year, counted by the due date or by the landed date (a pay due Sat 1 Jan moved to Fri 31 Dec)? And which year's count does a period that starts in December and ends in January use?
open.ref_does: calendar year, by the due date before any move; a period uses the year it starts in

open.question: Which pays get the extra minor unit when a year does not divide evenly (the first ones, the last ones, spread through the year)?
open.ref_does: spread: pay k gets floor(year x k / N) - floor(year x (k - 1) / N)

open.question: The first year of a schedule set up in November: "26 or 27" counts the whole year by its rhythm, but the schedule has only 4 pays in that year. Which count?
open.ref_does: the whole year by its rhythm (26 or 27), counted back from its first date

open.question: `per: week` when days / 7 is not whole (5,000 over 30 days = 21,428.57): how is it rounded, and must a year of periods add up?
open.ref_does: half up per period, nothing carried

open.question: No fixed pay: 365 or 366 days in a leap year, how a day's amount is rounded (lookahead_ref.js carries the remainder so nothing is lost), and what `per: pay` and `per: week` mean with no fixed pay.
open.ref_does: 365; the total over the days is rounded down once; `per: pay` refuses, `per: week` is amount / 7 a day

open.question: Confirm: lookahead_ref.js `paysAYear` uses 52 / n (26 flat for every two weeks, 52 for weekly) and rounds each period on its own, so a year does not add up. It is the model's plain form only; the engine takes the count and the spread from this file.
open.ref_does: the real count and the spread

open.question: A saved amount that is not a whole number (an old or hand-edited copy): kept as is, refused, or asked about? Section 0 says nothing is rounded on load.
